entry: American adult animated science fiction sitcom. Created by Justin Roiland and Dan Harmon for [[Adult Swim]], the series follows Rick Sanchez, a cynical scientist, and his grandson Morty Smith through interdimensional adventures that alternate with domestic family life. Roiland initially voiced both title characters; Adult Swim cut ties with him in 2023 amid allegations of domestic abuse, and Ian Cardoni and Harry Belden were recast from the seventh season. It grew out of an animated *Back to the Future* parody made for Channel 101. It won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Animated Program twice, in 2018 and 2020.

Internet meme and bait-and-switch prank. It uses a disguised hyperlink to the music video for "Never Gonna Give You Up" (1987) by English singer [[Rick Astley]]. It began on May 15, 2007, when a user uploaded the video to [[YouTube]] and linked to it in place of a trailer for *Grand Theft Auto IV*. It peaked in 2008, when YouTube used it for its April Fools' Day event. Later pranksters included U.S. Representative [[Nancy Pelosi]] in 2009 and the Twitter account of the [[White House]] in 2011. By 2021 the official video had been viewed over one billion times.

Two- or three-wheeled passenger [[Cart|cart]], originally pulled by one person. The word comes from the Japanese *jinrikisha*, meaning "human-powered vehicle." The first known use of the term in English was in 1879. The most widely accepted account credits Izumi Yosuke, Suzuki Tokujiro and Takayama Kosuke with inventing the vehicle in Tokyo in 1869, although other claims exist and the origin remains unclear. Pulled rickshaws were a popular form of transport and a source of work for male laborers in Asian cities in the 19th century, but they declined as cars and trains became widely available. Cycle rickshaws (also called pedicabs or trishaws), auto rickshaws and electric rickshaws have replaced most pulled rickshaws, which survive mainly in tourism. Bangladesh has the highest number of rickshaws in the world, with 40,000 operating daily in the capital [[Dhaka]]. In 2023, [[UNESCO]] listed rickshaws and rickshaw art as "intangible heritage" of Bangladesh.

English comedian, actor, writer and director. With Stephen Merchant he co-created the [[BBC]] sitcoms *The Office* (2001–2003) and *Extras* (2005–2007), and he later created *After Life* (2019–2022). Gervais initially worked in the music industry as singer of the new-wave act Seona Dancing, and he began stand-up comedy in the late 1990s. He has performed five multinational stand-up tours. His films include the *Night at the Museum* series and *Special Correspondents*, released by [[Netflix]] in 2016. He has received seven British Academy Television Awards and two Primetime Emmy Awards, and he hosted the Golden Globe Awards five times.

Puerto Rican singer and songwriter. He began as a member of the boy band Menudo and started his solo career in 1991. His English-language album *Ricky Martin* (1999) was his first to top the *Billboard* 200, and its lead single "Livin' la Vida Loca" topped the Billboard Hot 100 and the UK Singles Chart. He won his first [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for *Vuelve* (1998). He has sold over 70 million records worldwide. He acted in the soap opera [[General Hospital]]. His activism focuses on LGBT rights and on [[Human trafficking|human trafficking]], and in 2004 he founded The Ricky Martin Foundation.

American musician and actor. From age eight he appeared with his family in the radio and television series *The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet*. He began his recording career in 1957 and placed 54 songs on the Billboard Hot 100. "Poor Little Fool" (1958) was the first number-one song on the Hot 100. He appeared in the [[Western (genre)|western]] *Rio Bravo* (1959) with [[John Wayne]] and [[Dean Martin]]. His 1972 single "Garden Party" peaked at number six on the Hot 100. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1987. He died in a plane crash.

Statement, question or phrase with a double or veiled meaning, posed as a puzzle. Riddles are of two main types: enigmas, which use metaphorical language and require careful thought, and conundrums, which rely on punning. Archer Taylor called riddling "a universal art" and cited riddles from many cultures. The English word shares its origin with *read*, from a Common Germanic verb meaning "to interpret" or "guess." In 1963 Robert A. Georges and Alan Dundes defined a riddle as a traditional verbal expression with descriptive elements, the referent of which is to be guessed. In Greek myth the [[Sphinx]] posed a riddle to Oedipus. [[Aristotle]] wrote that "metaphors imply riddles." Scholars have also argued that riddles play with conceptual boundaries while ultimately affirming social norms.

English filmmaker known for science fiction and historical epic films. Scott began in television and advertising before making his feature debut with *The Duellists* (1977). He gained wide recognition with *Alien* (1979) and *Blade Runner* (1982). His later films include *Gladiator* (2000), set in 2nd-century [[Rome]], and *Black Hawk Down* (2001). He has been nominated for the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Director three times. He is the eighth-highest-grossing director of all time, with films grossing a cumulative $5 billion worldwide. [[Elizabeth II|Queen Elizabeth II]] knighted him in 2003, and [[Charles III]] appointed him a Knight Grand Cross in 2024.

Conjecture about the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. The hypothesis states that all nontrivial zeros of the [[Riemann zeta function]] lie on the critical line, where the real part is 1/2. The zeta function has trivial zeros at the negative even integers, so the conjecture concerns the other zeros. [[Bernhard Riemann]] proposed it in his 1859 paper "On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude." It is of great interest in [[Number theory|number theory]] because it implies results about the distribution of [[Prime number|prime numbers]]. Many consider it the most important unsolved problem in [[Pure mathematics|pure mathematics]]. It is one of the [[Millennium Prize Problems]], which carry a US$1 million prize. It forms part of the eighth of [[David Hilbert]]'s 23 unsolved problems. Numerical checks confirm it for the first 10¹³ nontrivial zeros, but no proof is known.

Connected one-dimensional complex manifold. Riemann surfaces, first studied by and named after [[Bernhard Riemann]], can be thought of as deformed versions of the complex plane: locally they resemble patches of the plane, but their global shape can differ. A [[Sphere|sphere]], a [[Torus|torus]] and several sheets glued together are examples. They include graphs of multivalued functions such as log(z), which become single-valued on the surface. A two-dimensional real surface can be turned into a Riemann surface if and only if it is orientable and metrizable. The sphere and torus admit such structures, but the [[Möbius strip]] and the Klein bottle do not. Every compact Riemann surface is a complex algebraic curve, by Chow's theorem and the Riemann–Roch theorem.

Complex function central to analytic number theory. It is defined by the series ζ(s) = Σ 1/nˢ for complex s with real part greater than 1, and extended analytically to the rest of the complex plane. [[Leonhard Euler]] studied it over the real numbers in the first half of the 18th century. [[Bernhard Riemann]]'s 1859 paper extended it to complex variables and linked its zeros to the distribution of primes, the subject of the [[Riemann hypothesis]]. Roger Apéry proved the irrationality of ζ(3) in 1979. The function has applications in [[Physics|physics]], probability theory and [[Statistics|applied statistics]].

Branch of differential geometry that studies Riemannian manifolds. It studies smooth manifolds equipped with a Riemannian metric, a smoothly varying inner product on each tangent space, which defines length, angle, surface area and volume locally. Distances are measured along curves, as an insect crawling over a surface would measure them. The field originated with the vision of [[Bernhard Riemann]], expressed in his inaugural lecture "On the Hypotheses Which Lie at the Foundations of Geometry." It generalizes the differential geometry of surfaces to higher dimensions. Its development enabled the formulation of [[General relativity|Einstein's general theory of relativity]], and it made a profound impact on group theory, representation theory, analysis and topology.

Smooth manifold equipped with a Riemannian metric. The metric is a smoothly varying inner product on each tangent space, and from it calculus yields distance, curvature and parallel transport. [[Euclidean space]], the n-sphere, hyperbolic space and smooth surfaces such as ellipsoids are examples. [[Bernhard Riemann]] first described these spaces in his June 10, 1854, inaugural lecture. John Nash proved that every Riemannian manifold can be realized as a submanifold of Euclidean space, but the intrinsic viewpoint defines geometric notions without reference to an ambient space. Applications include physics, especially [[General relativity|general relativity]] and gauge theory, as well as computer graphics, machine learning and [[Cartography|cartography]].

Long-barreled [[Firearm|firearm]] designed for accurate shooting, with a barrel cut by helical grooves called rifling. The raised areas between the grooves, called lands, grip the projectile and spin it. The spin persists after the projectile leaves the barrel and gives it gyroscopic stability through conservation of angular momentum, which increases accuracy and effective range. Rifling distinguished rifles from smoothbore weapons such as [[Arquebus|arquebuses]] and [[Musket|muskets]]. Some of the earliest European experiments with rifling were carried out in the 15th century. Propellants were originally black powder and are now [[Nitrocellulose|nitrocellulose]] and other smokeless powders. Rifles are used in warfare, law enforcement, hunting and target shooting. Modern military rifles are magazine-fed, while [[Machine gun|machine guns]] are generally belt-fed.

Capital and largest city of [[Latvia]] (pop., 2026: 588,911), on the Gulf of Riga where the Daugava river meets the [[Baltic Sea]]. Founded in 1201, Riga was a member of the [[Hanseatic League]], and its historical center is a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site noted for its Art Nouveau architecture. The city was the European Capital of Culture in 2014, together with Umeå in Sweden. It hosted the 2006 NATO Summit and the Eurovision Song Contest 2003. Riga is home to the office of the European Union's Body of European Regulators for Electronic Communications (BEREC). Riga International Airport is the largest and busiest airport in the Baltic States. In 2019 Riga received over 1.4 million foreign visitors.

Blue [[Supergiant|supergiant]] star in the constellation [[Orion (constellation)|Orion]]. Designated Beta Orionis, Rigel is the brightest star in Orion and generally the seventh-brightest star in the night sky. It is the brightest and most massive member of a system of at least four stars, about 850 light-years away. Its surface temperature is 12,100 K and its radius is more than 70 times that of the Sun. It is calculated to be 61,500 to 363,000 times as luminous as the Sun and 18 to 24 times as massive. With an estimated age of seven to nine million years, Rigel has exhausted its core hydrogen. It is expected to end as a [[Supernova|Type II supernova]], leaving a neutron star or a black hole.

[[Angle]] of exactly 90 degrees (π/2 radians), equal to a quarter turn. The term is a calque of the Latin *angulus rectus*, in which *rectus* means "upright." Two lines that meet at a right angle are perpendicular. A right angle is the defining feature of a right triangle, which makes it basic to [[Trigonometry]]. A [[Square]] has four right angles, as does a rectangle, a [[Quadrilateral|quadrilateral]]. The [[Pythagorean theorem]] states when a triangle is a right triangle. [[Euclid's Elements]] treats all right angles as equal in Postulate 4, which allows a right angle to serve as a unit for measuring other angles. Carpenters and masons have long checked for a right angle with the 3-4-5 rule, based on the Pythagorean triple (3, 4, 5).

Mnemonic convention for orientations and rotations in three-dimensional space. In mathematics and physics it defines the direction of the [[Cross product|cross product]] of two vectors and the orientation of coordinate axes. In electromagnetism it gives the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a [[Magnetic field|magnetic field]]. The convention is often credited to [[William Rowan Hamilton]]. After debate, the mainstream shifted to the three-vector system of [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]], which led to the prevalent adoption of the rule. John Fleming introduced the physics form in the late 19th century.

Political ideologies that view social stratification and orders as inevitable, natural or desirable. Right-wing politics typically supports conservatism, natural law, authority, property, religion and tradition, and often favors [[Laissez-faire|laissez-faire]] economic policies. It is the counterpart of [[Left-wing politics|left-wing politics]], and the [[Political spectrum|left–right political spectrum]] is the most common. The terms originated during the [[French Revolution]], when supporters of the old order sat to the right of the presiding officer of the National Assembly. [[Edmund Burke]] is regarded as one of the most influential conservative thinkers of the 18th century. Both "right" and "right-wing" have been used as compliments and as pejoratives.

Political ideology that combines right-wing politics with populist rhetoric. Its rhetoric is anti-elitist and claims to speak for common people, and its themes include neo-nationalism, social conservatism, economic nationalism and fiscal conservatism. Some have associations with authoritarianism, and some far-right populists have been compared to [[Fascism|fascism]]. In Europe the term often describes parties known for opposition to immigration and for Euroscepticism. Political scientist Cas Mudde rejects nationalism as the core of the ideology and prefers nativism. Right-wing populism has remained the dominant political force in the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] since the 2010s. Examples include [[Donald Trump]] and [[Marine Le Pen]].

Legal, social or ethical principles of freedom or entitlement. Rights are the fundamental normative rules about what is allowed or owed to people under a legal system, social convention or ethical theory. They are central to law, ethics and theories of [[Justice|justice]]. A prevailing view once held that the ancient world had no concept of rights, a view since challenged. Natural rights are universal and considered inalienable, while legal rights rest on a society's laws, such as the right to vote. Citizenship has been defined as the "right to have rights." [[Thomas Aquinas]] held that positive law not grounded in natural law conferred no rights in the proper sense, while [[Jeremy Bentham]] regarded legal rights as the essence of rights and denied natural rights.

Barbadian singer, songwriter, businesswoman and actress. Born in Saint Michael, [[Barbados]], she is one of the best-selling music artists, with estimated sales exceeding 250 million records. *Good Girl Gone Bad* (2007) made her a major star, with the number-one singles "Umbrella" and "Take a Bow." She topped the Billboard 200 with *Unapologetic* (2012) and *Anti* (2016). She has won nine [[Grammy Awards]] and has 14 number-one singles on the Billboard Hot 100. She founded the cosmetics brand Fenty Beauty, and the fashion brand Fenty operates under [[LVMH]]. The government of Barbados made her a National Hero in 2021.

[[Planetary nebula|Planetary nebula]] in the constellation [[Lyra]]. Also cataloged as Messier 57 (M57) and NGC 6720, it lies south of [[Vega]], about midway between the stars Beta and Gamma Lyrae. Charles Messier discovered it in 1779. Its apparent visual magnitude is 8.8, too faint for the naked eye but readily seen with a small telescope. A planetary nebula forms when a star expels a shell of ionized gas before becoming a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]]. The central star of this nebula is a carbon-oxygen white dwarf about 2,570 light-years from the Sun. After expanding for 1,610 years, the nebula is about 1 light-year in diameter.

1998 Japanese supernatural psychological horror film directed by Hideo Nakata. Based on the 1991 novel by Koji Suzuki, it follows a reporter investigating a cursed videotape that kills whoever watches it after seven days. It was shot back to back with its sequel, *Spiral*. The film was a box office hit and was acclaimed by critics for its atmosphere and slow-paced horror. It spawned a franchise and helped popularize Japanese horror in the West, notably through the English-language remake *The Ring* (2002). Its success also led to a renaissance of Japanese horror films, including *Ju-On* and *One Missed Call*.

Algebraic structure with addition and multiplication. A ring is a set with two binary operations, addition and multiplication, such that it is an [[Abelian group|abelian group]] under addition, multiplication is associative, and multiplication distributes over addition. Many authors also require a multiplicative identity. Multiplication need not be [[Commutative ring|commutative]]. Every field, the integers and polynomials are examples of commutative rings, while n × n matrices with n ≥ 2 are noncommutative. Rings were first formalized as generalizations of Dedekind domains and polynomial rings. Ring theory developed from the 1870s to the 1920s, with contributions from [[Richard Dedekind]], [[David Hilbert]] and [[Emmy Noether]]. Rings are basic tools in [[Algebraic geometry|algebraic geometry]] and [[Algebraic number theory|algebraic number theory]].
